initialLogin.welcomeDescription: This is your main workspace where you can browse, manage, and organize all the objects in your system. Objects are the core entities that represent real-world items, documents, or concepts you want to track and manage.
initialLogin.processesDescription: Here you can track and monitor processes that transform or move your objects. This section helps you understand how objects flow through different stages, from input to output, giving you complete visibility into your operational workflows.
initialLogin.sharesDescription: Bundle objects and hand them to other people. Replaces Groups — a Share carries resources, and lists who can see them.
initialLogin.libraryDescription: Your reusable definitions: Templates to start an object from, Formulas to compute values, and Constants they can refer to.
initialLogin.importDescription: Import existing data from external sources, spreadsheets, or other systems. This powerful feature allows you to bring your legacy data into IoM efficiently, supporting various formats and bulk operations to get you started quickly.
initialLogin.searchDescription: Use the powerful search functionality to quickly find any object, process, or data across your entire IoM workspace. Press Cmd+K (or Ctrl+K) to open the command center and search through everything with intelligent filtering and suggestions.
initialLogin.demoTourDescription: Ready for a hands-on experience? Click "Demo tour" anytime to take a comprehensive walkthrough that will guide you through creating your first object, exploring all the features, and understanding how everything works together.

demo.filtersDescription: Narrow the list — including whether deleted objects are shown. Nothing here is ever destroyed: a deleted object stays in place, struck through, and can be restored at any time.
demo.viewOptionsDescription: Switch between different view modes to see your data in the format that works best for you. Choose from table view for detailed listings or column view for a more visual, card-based layout. Your preference is automatically saved.
demo.createObjectsDescription: This is where your object creation journey begins. Click this button anytime you want to add a new object to your IoM system. Objects can represent anything from physical items to digital assets, processes, or concepts.
demo.modelTemplatesDescription: Choose from predefined templates that automatically populate relevant fields based on the type of object you're creating. Models ensure consistency and save time by providing structured blueprints for common object types in your organization.
demo.parentRelationshipsDescription: Place this object under others in the hierarchy. The hierarchy is parents-only — a child records who its parent is, so moving something never touches the object it used to sit under.
demo.objectMetadataDescription: These core fields define your object's identity: Name (the primary identifier), Abbreviation (optional short code for quick reference), Version (for tracking changes over time), and Description (detailed explanation for team understanding). Fill these thoughtfully as they're used throughout the system for search and identification.
demo.locationInfoDescription: Associate a physical address or location with your object when relevant. This is particularly useful for tracking assets, facilities, or any objects that have a geographic component to their identity.
demo.fileAttachmentsDescription: Upload supporting documents, images, specifications, or any files that provide additional context about your object. These attachments become part of the object's permanent record and are searchable within the system.
demo.customPropertiesDescription: Add specialized data fields unique to your object. Each property has a name and value, and you can attach files to individual properties for detailed documentation. This flexibility allows you to capture any specific information your object needs.
demo.completeCreationDescription: When you've filled in all the necessary information, click Create to save your new object to the system. The object will then be available for searching, linking, and use in processes throughout your IoM workspace.

createProcess.startDescription: A process records something that happened — a step that took objects in and produced others. This button opens the create sheet; Next opens it for you.
createProcess.templateDescription: A process template pre-fills the properties this kind of process usually records, so you are not typing the same fields each time. Skip it and start blank if none fit.
createProcess.detailsDescription: The name is how the process reads everywhere else — in the list, and as a node in the flow diagram. Something specific beats something clever.
createProcess.propertiesDescription: Properties hold what you measured about this process — a temperature, a duration, a cost. Values can be typed in or derived from a formula.
createProcess.flowsDescription: These tabs are where a process says what it consumed and what it produced. A process needs at least one of each before it will save, so open them before saving — walking the flows themselves is a separate tour.
createProcess.saveDescription: Saved processes appear in the list and connect to the objects they reference, which is what draws the flow diagram.

buildTemplate.startDescription: A template is a starting point for new objects — the properties they begin with, including formula recipes and the constants those bind to. This button offers object and process templates; Next opens an object one to build.
buildTemplate.propertiesDescription: Whatever you add here is what a new object starts with. A property bound to a formula brings that binding along, not just the field name.
buildTemplate.saveDescription: Once saved it appears at the top of the create sheet for every new object, ready to pick.

writeFormula.referenceDescription: The reference lists every function and operator available, plus how to refer to other properties and to constants.
writeFormula.startDescription: A formula is an expression bound to a property value and recomputed server-side.
writeFormula.expressionDescription: Formulas are immutable once saved — changing one means duplicating it and binding the new version, so anything already using the old one keeps its meaning.

shareObjects.tabsDescription: Shares are the bundles you built. Direct shares lists what you granted on a single item on its own. Each tab edits only its own kind — a bundle is always changed on the bundle.
shareObjects.startDescription: A share bundles resources and grants a group access to all of them at once.
shareObjects.resourcesDescription: Add what you want to share — objects and processes, or formulas, constants and templates, but never both kinds in one bundle. Access cascades to an object's children, and the whole bundle can be revoked in one step.
shareObjects.membersDescription: A share carries only resources and lists its members here — that is the difference from the Groups it replaced, which mixed both under one word.

defineConstant.whatDescription: A CO₂ factor, a density, a tax rate — written once here instead of typed into twenty formulas. When the figure changes you edit this one row, and every formula bound to it follows. The node ships some already; the ones you make are yours to share.
defineConstant.startDescription: Next opens the form. There are only two fields, and the second one is the interesting half.
defineConstant.name: The name is the binding
defineConstant.nameDescription: This is what a formula reaches for — you pick it from a Constants list in the formula editor rather than typing a number. It cannot be renamed later: a binding records the name, so a rename would orphan every calculation using it.
defineConstant.valueDescription: A plain number, or a number with a unit: 0.42, 10 kg, 3.5 m. The unit travels with the value, so a formula that mixes this with metres knows what it is holding.
defineConstant.saveDescription: Saving publishes the first version. Changing the value afterwards does not overwrite it — it publishes a NEW one, and every formula keeps the version it was bound to. That is the point of a constant: a number you can correct without silently changing results someone already recorded.

rollUpValues.whatDescription: Rooms carry a floor area. A rule for that property makes every floor show the sum of its rooms, and every building the sum of all its floors — with no number authored anywhere in between. A formula works across one object's own values; this is the only thing that reaches DOWN the tree. Rules are not attached to an object: you name a property once and it applies to all of yours.
rollUpValues.startDescription: The node already ships rules for the common keys — weight, volume, area, cost. Next opens the form to add your own.
rollUpValues.keysDescription: Type the key and press Add — it becomes a chip, and you can queue several before saving, which creates one rule each. Nothing happens on submit until a chip exists. Keys are stored lower-case, so "Mass" and "mass" are the same rule. If the key usually holds text you will see a warning; it does not stop you, but the total will stay empty.
rollUpValues.saveDescription: This is the part that looks like a bug and is not. A rule only counts writes made after it exists — added to data that already landed, it stays quiet until the next change anywhere below. The total then appears on the PARENT, as a dashed "Derived" card, within about a minute. A leaf with no children shows no card at all.

runImport.jobsDescription: A row per job, with its status and how many rows landed. Open one to see what happened row by row — including which ones the node refused, and why.
runImport.startDescription: The same page holds both views. Next switches to the wizard; the results stay here and keep updating while you work.
runImport.stepsDescription: Upload, pick a sheet, map the columns, check, import. Next loads a small example file so you can see all five — nothing of yours is touched, and it is thrown away when this walkthrough ends.
runImport.sheetDescription: A workbook can hold several sheets, and a real export often begins with a title or a blank line. Mark the header row and the first data row on the grid itself, so you read the answer where you asked the question.
runImport.columnsDescription: The dropdown on the right of each row says what that column becomes: the object's name, a part of its address, a property, or nothing at all. Unmapped columns are simply not imported. A column mapped to a property gets a second dropdown for splitting one cell into several values, for sheets that pack a list into `a; b; c`.
runImport.hierarchyDescription: By default one row becomes one object. But a sheet often repeats a container down a column — the same building on every one of its rooms. Turning those columns into LEVELS builds the tree instead. Nothing here guesses on its own, because a wrong guess merges data away silently. Next asks for a proposal.
runImport.proposalDescription: The columns it names tell you very little — a real hierarchy and two unrelated categories look identical in the data. What it would produce does not: "200 rows would become 3 objects" is wrong at a glance. Read the count, then accept or refuse. Next accepts it.
runImport.levelsDescription: Buildings and floors are now containers, not repeated text, and the count above says how many objects that makes. Every column that is NOT a level has just gained a third dropdown — "attaches to" — because a value now has to say which level it belongs to: the deepest one, a named one, or all of them. An address usually belongs to all of them.
runImport.checkDescription: The count, the tree it will build, and every row the wizard already knows it cannot use. Nothing has been sent yet. You can pick a parent object here, so the whole import lands somewhere in your structure.
runImport.runDescription: The button below the card starts it. The job runs in the background and reports per row, so you can leave this page. The walkthrough stops here — this is example data, and it will be cleared when you close this.

workWithDrafts.start: Start something you can finish later
workWithDrafts.startDescription: Open the create sheet as usual. Nothing is saved to the server until you submit.
workWithDrafts.fillDescription: Close the sheet with unsaved changes and you are offered a draft. It waits pinned above the objects list until you come back — on this device only, and files you picked are not carried over.
